gloss_terse: To cut in, inscribe, or engrave; by extension, to decree or enact laws; as a substantive, a ruler, lawgiver, or the scepter symbolizing authority.
gloss_readable: A richly layered verb whose core image is the act of cutting marks into a hard surface — stone, metal, or tablet. From this physical act of engraving flows the metaphor of inscribing law: one who carves decrees into stone becomes the lawgiver, and the staff he holds becomes the scepter of authority. In Genesis 49:10 Jacob prophesies that the scepter (mᵉḥoqēq) will not depart from Judah, while in Isaiah 49:16 God declares 'I have engraved you on the palms of my hands' — the same verb moving from political authority to tender intimacy. The Spanish 'legislador' and 'cetro' neatly mirror this dual trajectory from engraver to ruler.

senses.1: The primary physical action: to cut, carve, or inscribe marks into a durable surface such as stone, metal, or clay. In Proverbs 8:27 Wisdom witnesses God inscribing a circle on the face of the deep at creation, while in Isaiah 30:8 the prophet is told to write on a tablet and engrave it in a book. The English glosses 'engrave' and 'inscribe' correspond to Spanish 'trazó' and 'decretó,' suggesting the act already shades toward authoritative marking.
senses.2: A metonymic extension where the Piel participle refers to the ruler's staff or scepter — the physical instrument of the one who engraves law. In Genesis 49:10 it appears alongside 'scepter' (šēbeṭ), and in Numbers 21:18 the nobles dig a well 'with the scepter' (bimḥoqēq). Spanish 'cetro' and German 'Zepter' capture this concrete object sense, while the underlying metaphor links carved authority to the rod of office.
senses.3: Used substantively for the person who enacts legislation: the lawgiver, ruler, or commander. Deuteronomy 33:21 speaks of a commander's portion reserved for the lawgiver, and Judges 5:9 celebrates Israel's commanders (ḥoqᵉqê) who volunteered for battle. Spanish 'legislador' and 'legisladores' consistently render this human-agent sense, distinguishing it from the instrument (sense 2) and the act of decreeing (sense 4).
senses.4: The verbal act of issuing decrees or enacting statutes with binding force. In Proverbs 8:15 wisdom declares 'by me kings reign and rulers decree what is just,' and in Isaiah 10:1 the prophet pronounces woe upon 'those who decree iniquitous decrees.' Spanish 'decretan' and 'lo-decretado' highlight the legislative act itself rather than the agent or instrument.
senses.5: The passive result of engraving: to be carved or inscribed upon a surface. Job 19:23 expresses the wish that his words 'be inscribed in a book' and engraved with an iron stylus, while Ezekiel 23:14 describes figures of Chaldeans engraved on a wall. This Qal passive participle and Hofal usage presents the completed state of the inscription rather than the active process.

gloss_terse: To throw or cast upon; to lay hands on (seize); to place upon; of waves, to beat against; reflexively, to reflect upon; of a share, to fall to someone.
gloss_readable: A versatile compound verb (epi + ballō, 'throw upon') whose range stretches from violent arrest to quiet reflection. Its most frequent New Testament usage involves laying hands on someone to seize them, as when the temple guards attempt to arrest Jesus in John 7:30. But the same verb describes placing garments on a colt (Mark 11:7), waves crashing over a boat in a Galilean storm (Mark 4:37), and — most memorably — Peter's anguished weeping when the cock crows (Mark 14:72). Spanish captures the emotional nuance with 'habiendo pensado en ello' (having reflected on it), while the physical senses cluster around 'echar' (to throw, cast).

senses.1: To lay hands upon someone with hostile intent, typically to arrest or seize them by force. This is the dominant New Testament usage, appearing ten times in contexts of persecution and attempted arrest. In Matthew 26:50 the crowd lays hands on Jesus in Gethsemane, and in Luke 21:12 Jesus warns his disciples that people will lay hands on them. Spanish consistently uses 'echar mano' (to cast hands) and 'echaron' (they cast/seized), preserving the compound verb's literal force of throwing one's hands upon another.
senses.2: To put, place, or cast something upon a surface or person in a non-hostile, practical sense. Jesus speaks of no one putting a new patch on an old garment (Matt 9:16, Luke 5:36), the disciples throw their cloaks on the colt (Mark 11:7), and in Luke 9:62 no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom. Spanish 'pone' (places) and 'echan sobre' (cast upon) reflect the gentler physical action.
senses.3: Of natural forces — particularly waves — crashing against or breaking over something. In Mark 4:37 a great windstorm arises and the waves 'were beating into' (epeballen) the boat so that it was filling up. Spanish 'golpeaban' (they were striking) captures the violent, repetitive force of the sea, a sense unique to this single occurrence.
senses.4: A striking intransitive or reflexive usage meaning to set one's mind upon something and break down emotionally. In Mark 14:72, after the rooster crows a second time, Peter 'epibalōn' — variously translated as 'when he thought thereon' or 'having broken down' — wept bitterly. Spanish 'habiendo pensado en ello' emphasizes the cognitive moment of reflection, while many interpreters see the physical gesture of covering one's head or collapsing. This hapax-like sense remains debated among commentators.
senses.5: An impersonal or middle usage meaning 'to fall to one's share,' referring to the portion of an inheritance or property that belongs to someone. In Luke 15:12 the younger son asks for the share of the estate 'falling' (epiballon) to him. Spanish 'que me corresponde' (that corresponds to me) and German 'zufallen' capture this distributive, almost legal sense of what is owed or allotted.

gloss_terse: To hold fast, retain; to restrain or suppress; to possess or occupy; passively, to be held or bound; nautically, to head toward a destination.
gloss_readable: Built from kata + echō ('hold down'), this verb carries the core image of maintaining a firm grip — whether on a cherished tradition or on a person one will not release. Paul urges the Thessalonians to 'hold fast what is good' (1 Thess 5:21), while in Romans 1:18 the wicked 'suppress the truth in unrighteousness.' The same word describes possessing property (2 Cor 6:10), being held captive by illness (John 5:4), and steering a ship toward shore (Acts 27:40). Spanish distinguishes beautifully between 'retener' (to retain, hold fast) and 'retenían' (they were holding back), while 'se dirigían' (they were heading) captures the nautical extension.

senses.1: To hold firmly onto something valuable — faith, tradition, teaching, or moral conviction — and refuse to let it go. In Luke 8:15 the good soil represents those who hear the word and 'hold it fast' in an honest heart, and in 1 Corinthians 11:2 Paul commends the church for holding to the traditions he delivered. Spanish 'retened' (hold fast, imperative) and 'retener' (to retain) emphasize the active, intentional grip on what is received. Philemon 1:13 shows the personal dimension: Paul would have liked to 'keep' Onesimus with him.
senses.2: To hold back, restrain, or suppress something or someone from acting, advancing, or becoming known. Romans 1:18 declares God's wrath against those who 'suppress' (katechontōn) the truth, while 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7 speaks of a mysterious restrainer who holds back the man of lawlessness. In Luke 4:42 the crowds tried to 'hold' Jesus and keep him from leaving. Spanish 'que retienen' (who suppress) and 'que detiene' (who restrains) reflect the forceful withholding.
senses.3: To possess, occupy, or have as one's own — whether a physical seat, property, or status. In Luke 14:9 a guest is told to take the lowest place lest the host say 'give this man your seat,' and in 1 Corinthians 7:30 Paul counsels that those who buy should live as though they do not 'possess.' The paradox of 2 Corinthians 6:10, 'having nothing, yet possessing all things,' plays on this sense. Spanish 'poseyendo' (possessing) and 'ocupar' (to occupy) capture both the abstract and spatial dimensions.
senses.4: In the passive voice, to be held, bound, or gripped by an affliction, obligation, or spiritual condition. John 5:4 describes those 'held' by various diseases at the pool of Bethesda, and Romans 7:6 speaks of having been released from the law that formerly 'held us.' Spanish 'era poseído' (was possessed/held) and 'éramos retenidos' (we were held) convey the involuntary, constrained state.
senses.5: A nautical technical term meaning to steer or hold a course toward a destination. In Acts 27:40 the sailors cut the anchors, hoisted the foresail, and 'made for' (kateichon) the beach. Spanish 'se dirigían' (they were heading) captures the directional intent, and the underlying image remains consistent: holding the ship firmly on its course, applying the 'hold down' force to navigation.

gloss_terse: To stink, emit a foul odor; causatively, to cause something to stink; figuratively, to make odious or bring into disrepute; to become or make oneself abhorrent.
gloss_readable: A pungently vivid verb whose literal meaning — to emit a foul stench — anchors some of the Bible's most memorable scenes: the Nile reeking with dead fish during the plagues (Exod 7:18), manna crawling with worms overnight (Exod 16:20), and dead flies spoiling the perfumer's oil (Eccl 10:1). From this sensory root grows a powerful social metaphor: to 'make someone stink' is to ruin their reputation. Jacob fears his sons have made him 'stink' among the Canaanites after the Shechem massacre (Gen 34:30), and David's servants worry they have become 'odious' to the Ammonites (2 Sam 10:6). Spanish tracks the literal-figurative divide with 'apestar' (to stink) versus 'hacer heder' (to make stinking/odious).

senses.1: The Hifil causative used figuratively: to make someone odious, detestable, or repugnant in another's estimation — to destroy their social standing or reputation. In Genesis 34:30 Jacob tells Simeon and Levi 'you have made me stink (hib'ashtem) among the inhabitants of the land,' and in Exodus 5:21 the Israelite foremen accuse Moses of making them 'stink in the eyes of Pharaoh.' Proverbs 13:5 uses the Hifil of the righteous who 'make shameful' versus the wicked. Spanish 'hacer heder' (to make stinking) and French 'faisant-lui-même-odieux' preserve the causative social dimension.
senses.2: The Qal stem in its primary physical sense: to stink, to emit a foul odor from decay or putrefaction. The plague narratives of Exodus provide the classic examples — the Nile stinks from dead fish (7:18, 7:21), the land reeks from heaps of dead frogs (8:14), and hoarded manna becomes wormy and foul (16:20). Isaiah 50:2 uses the same image prophetically: fish stink for lack of water. Spanish 'apestar' and 'apestó' capture the direct olfactory revulsion, while the consistent appearance across Exodus source documents (E, J, P) shows its centrality to plague narrative vocabulary.
senses.3: The Hifil with literal rather than figurative force: to cause something to physically emit a foul odor. Exodus 16:24 contrasts with 16:20 — manna kept as God commanded did not 'cause stench' (lō hib'ish). Psalm 38:5 describes festering wounds that 'stink and are corrupt,' and Ecclesiastes 10:1 warns that dead flies 'cause the perfumer's ointment to stink.' Spanish 'hacen heder' (they make stinking) and German 'stink' mark this as causative but still within the realm of physical smell, distinguishing it from the social-reputational Hifil of sense 1.
senses.4: The Nifal (passive/reflexive) stem: to become odious or detested in someone's eyes, a figurative extension from physical stench to social revulsion experienced as something that happens to the subject. In 1 Samuel 13:4 the Israelites 'had become odious' (nib'ash) to the Philistines, and in 2 Samuel 10:6 the Ammonites realize they 'had become odious' to David. Spanish 'se hicieron odiosos' (they made themselves odious) and French 'devint-odieux' capture the Nifal's sense of the stench of disgrace settling upon someone.
senses.5: The Hitpael (reflexive-causative) stem: to make oneself odious, to bring disgrace upon oneself through one's own deliberate actions. The single occurrence in 1 Chronicles 19:6 describes the Ammonites who recognized that they 'had made themselves odious' (hitba'ashū) to David by humiliating his ambassadors. Spanish 'se hicieron odiosos' parallels the Nifal rendering, but the Hitpael emphasizes self-inflicted damage to reputation — the subject is both agent and victim of the stench.
